stories.title: At least 37 dead and hundreds evacuated after strike on Kyiv warehouse
stories.summary: Thirty-seven people have been killed and almost 400 evacuated after a Russian drone strike triggered an explosion at a warehouse in the Kyiv region late on Friday. President Volodymyr Zelensky said the blast damaged residential buildings and a care home in the surrounding area, with an investigation launched into whether ammunition was being stored on site. Four children are among 42 people injured, according to regional head Tymur Tkachenko, with search and rescue operations ongoing at the site in the Bucha district early on Saturday. Zelensky wrote on X: "The regulations are clear: Ammunition must not be stored near houses or other residential buildings. Appropriate conclusions will certainly be drawn." He said more than 300 emergency service personnel had been deployed to the village of Myla, where "a care home for elderly people and people with disabilities" was among the properties damaged. "Criminal proceedings have been opened on charges of official negligence," he said. The office of Ukraine's prosecutor general said it was reviewing the "legality of the placement and storage of explosive objects and materials" near residential buildings. It said the "actions of officials who made the relevant decisions" would also be investigated. Russia's Ministry of Defence said in a statement that its forces had targeted "an ammunition depot" in Myla which stored "components and launch boosters for FP-1/FP-2 long-range unmanned aerial vehicles". Meanwhile, Tkachenko said a 14-year-old was killed in a separate attack in the Boryspil district while Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said a two-year-old had died after a Russian drone crashed in Obolonskyi. He added that five people, including an 18-year-old girl, were injured in fresh strikes on the capital on Saturday morning.

stories.title: Tour boss searches for missing brother and 54 pilgrims by air after Nepal floods
stories.summary: Gopal Thapa flew by helicopter to the flash flood area in northern Nepal to search for 55 missing pilgrims, including his brother, after the disaster on August 26. The group included 55 people of various nationalities, escorted by Leaf Holidays, and was caught at the Nepal-Tibet border during the flood. Thapa witnessed the destruction firsthand, expressed little hope for survivors, but still awaits news from Nepali authorities conducting rescue efforts. One of the first things that Gopal Thapa did when he heard about the flash flood on August 26 in northern Nepal was to fly straight into the disaster zone that very afternoon. The owner of Leaf Holidays, a Kathmandu-based travel and trekking agency, hired a chopper to try and trace 55 people, including four Singaporeans, who were part of a group that the agency was escorting to Tibet for the Kailash-Mansarovar pilgrimage. The group was inside the Gyoring Port complex on the Nepal-China border when Thapa, 42, last spoke with them on Wednesday morning. They had cleared immigration on the Nepali side and were queueing up to clear remaining formalities on the Tibetan side. Among those missing is his brother, Gokarna Thapa, 33, father of two children aged seven and one, who was leading the group, as well as eight other Nepalese staff from the agency. He has tried desperately each day to call their phones since Wednesday’s tragic flash flood but has not been able to get through. “It has been very painful,” he told. The Straits Times with a long pause. The 55-member group was an eclectic mix of nationalities, including 24 Malaysians, four Singaporeans, seven Ukrainians, an Italian, three Americans, two British, one Belarusian and 13 Nepalis (nine staff members and four clients).
